purpose: Map the current improved Moag edition and identify companion learning support without editing the transcription.
method: Inspected all lesson and minilesson headings, vocabulary/reading organization and exercise sections; sampled explanatory and contextual passages; inspected script tools, reference resources, digital guidance and the existing proofreading review. This is a curriculum support audit, not a sentence-by-sentence linguistic proofread, listening audit, learner trial or proficiency validation.
interpretation: Coverage and existing practice describe inspected material. Practical objectives, prerequisite links, priorities and proposed supplements are editorial judgments. Not identified means not found in the reviewed local edition, not proof that no external resource exists.

gaps.title: Independent feedback on exercises
gaps.scope: All 25 lessons; minilessons A–F as new practice is added
gaps.finding: Exercise models, translated examples and teacher/partner checking exist. No complete answer key with explanations of acceptable alternatives was identified; the digital guide explicitly says layout adaptation does not supply an answer key.
gaps.effect: Independent learners cannot reliably distinguish a valid alternative from a mistake, especially in open responses and translation.
gaps.proposal: Start with Lesson 1: original checks or companion answers with reasoning, common errors and acceptable variants. Separate fixed answers from sample open responses.
gaps.acceptance: Each pilot task has a verified model or answer, a short reason, and a clear note where other answers can be valid. Open tasks have a simple self-check rubric.

gaps.title: Match existing recordings to current lessons
gaps.scope: Lessons 1–25; coverage of script and minilessons unknown
gaps.finding: There are 25 lesson-named MP3s. Inventory metadata points to 1985; the text is the fourth edition. No section timestamp map or verified text alignment was identified. The digital edition does not claim a complete linked audio course.
gaps.effect: A track filename does not tell a learner which current dialogue, word list or exercise it supports.
gaps.proposal: Audit one track at a time against the current lesson, recording timestamps, matched sections, wording differences and uncovered sections. Decide on embedding or new recordings after alignment and reuse status are established.
gaps.acceptance: The pilot lesson has a section-to-timestamp map; unmatched sections are explicit. Audio availability and text alignment remain separate statuses.

gaps.title: Script practice alongside the first lessons
gaps.scope: Alphabet and symbols; Lessons 1–3, then later joining patterns
gaps.finding: The alphabet, reading-pattern exercises and 93 redrawn writing models are present. The usage guide advises learning the script as needed, but no task-sized entry sequence with independent recognition and writing checks was identified.
gaps.effect: A new learner must choose a manageable set of symbols and connect the models to actual lesson words.
gaps.proposal: Create a Lesson 1 script route using a limited symbol set, reading recognition, writing from a model, and reading without the model. Reuse existing diagram capabilities rather than commissioning replacement diagrams.
gaps.acceptance: Every practice word is glossed; required symbols are named; recognition and writing are checked separately. Learners can use paper, and digital writing is optional.

gaps.title: Smaller study units and prerequisites
gaps.finding: The book explicitly advises treating each substantial lesson as several sessions and offers both model-led and analytic study. Navigation and prerequisite notes have improved. No explicit per-session objective, practice selection and readiness check was identified.
gaps.effect: Learners still have to decide what to study today and whether they are ready for the next step.
gaps.proposal: Add a small companion route for each pilot lesson: objective, prerequisites, relevant explanation/model, selected practice and a short exit check. Mark reference material separately from first-pass requirements.
gaps.acceptance: A route states what the learner should do and how to check it. Time estimates are provisional, and it does not require reading every grammar note before speaking.

gaps.title: Choose forms by meaning and situation
gaps.priority: First for early contrasts then Later
gaps.finding: The source explains many contrasts and supplies examples and transformations. Form production is often easier to locate than independently checkable decisions about which form fits a new context.
gaps.effect: Correctly changing an ending does not demonstrate that a learner can choose the expression needed in an interaction.
gaps.proposal: Write original short situations with feedback: identity/existence, want/like, intention/future, giving, permission/ability, event sequence and tense/aspect. Use simple diagrams where they clarify case roles or timelines.
gaps.acceptance: Each contrast is backed by current reviewed explanations and speaker-checked examples. Feedback explains the meaning or context rather than only marking an ending wrong.

gaps.title: Dedicated practice for Lesson 14 structures
gaps.finding: The exercise section contains a newspaper-section response frame, plurals and reading items. Conditionals, either/or and relatives with possession/existence are explained and illustrated, but have little dedicated production practice in that section.
gaps.effect: The amount of practice does not match the range of new structures introduced.
gaps.proposal: Create three small original activities: conditional decisions, alternative choices, and descriptions identifying which person or object is meant. Add supported production after recognition.
gaps.acceptance: Each of the three objectives has recognition and production practice with feedback. The unclear all/each source prose is not used as an unqualified rule.

gaps.title: Use grammar to complete a communicative task
gaps.scope: Selected lessons, especially 11–13 and 15–24; minilesson A
gaps.finding: Classmate responses, introductions, number games, age exchanges, route drawing and itinerary writing already occur. Many later exercises primarily manipulate forms or translate sentences; spontaneous interaction needs teacher adaptation.
gaps.effect: Learners need a bridge from controlled practice to achieving a purpose with their own information.
gaps.proposal: Add one original task where useful: relay a message, resolve a schedule conflict, explain a route, describe an event, or compare options. Supply roles and enough language support for a partner or solo recording.
gaps.acceptance: The task has a practical outcome, uses supported vocabulary/forms, and includes a simple rubric for meaning and appropriateness. It extends existing interaction rather than claiming the course has none.

gaps.title: Independent pronunciation practice and feedback
gaps.scope: Alphabet; Lessons 1–12 and 20; minilessons B and G
gaps.finding: Explicit pronunciation work covers dental/alveolar/retroflex contrasts, aspiration, vowel and consonant length, nasals, laterals and rhotics. Several exercises require an instructor to speak or judge. The recordings have not been aligned to these activities.
gaps.effect: A print description alone cannot establish that a learner hears or produces a contrast.
gaps.proposal: After checking existing audio, supply short speaker-verified listening trials and spoken models for selected contrasts. Offer record-and-compare practice and specific partner/teacher feedback prompts.
gaps.acceptance: Listening trials have validated recordings and answers. Production is not auto-certified without a reliable assessment method; learners receive observable cues and a feedback route.

gaps.title: Cumulative retrieval and readiness checks
gaps.scope: Checkpoints after selected lesson groups; vocabulary across lessons
gaps.finding: The author recommends revisiting reading practice, and exercises reuse earlier forms. No explicit schedule of cumulative checks or learner progress record was identified in the inspected edition.
gaps.effect: Finishing a page does not show whether previously learned material is still usable.
gaps.proposal: Create original mixed review checks with feedback, delayed vocabulary retrieval and clear next-study suggestions. Keep these separate from claims of standardized proficiency levels.
gaps.acceptance: Checks mix recognition and production from prior lessons, revisit items after a delay, and identify what to review. Thresholds are pilot choices rather than validated proficiency cutoffs.

gaps.title: Vocabulary support by task and direction
gaps.scope: All lessons, reference lists and minilesson B
gaps.finding: Bilingual vocabulary and a Malayalam-to-English glossary exist. The author says extra grammar-example and reference vocabulary is not comprehensively included; current notes already gloss several confirmed early items. Search by English works, but that is not a curated reverse course vocabulary index.
gaps.effect: Learners may find a meaning without knowing which equivalent is appropriate or where it was practiced.
gaps.proposal: Maintain a curated course vocabulary record linking senses, supporting examples, relevant lesson and optional audio. Add English-side task lookup and short retrieval sets. Use Olam only where a specific gap exists and retain applicable attribution/license provenance.
gaps.acceptance: New items have a checked sense, context and provenance; introduction status distinguishes a glossed chunk from a fully taught form. Raw glossary lesson numbers are not treated as first-use proof.

gaps.title: Supported reading between dialogues and formal prose
gaps.finding: The course already contains formal geographical, newspaper and cultural prose, advertisements and comprehension work. It does not lack reading material. A separate ladder of short original passages with bounded vocabulary and independent feedback was not identified.
gaps.effect: Some learners would benefit from smaller passages before tackling the longer formal texts.
gaps.proposal: Write original short passages on familiar topics, with selective glosses, a few comprehension checks and a summary task. Link each to existing grammar and show spoken/formal alternatives when appropriate.
gaps.acceptance: Each passage states its prerequisite forms and glosses other language. Text and artwork are original or specifically licensed; school grade is not used as an L2 proficiency label.

gaps.title: Earlier listening bridges into casual speech
gaps.scope: Early dialogues, directions in Lesson 18 and minilesson G
gaps.finding: Early vocabulary and dialogues already include conversational short forms. Minilesson G explains several casual-speech changes but is placed after Lesson 24 and asks an instructor to model them.
gaps.effect: Learners encounter natural reductions well before reaching the dedicated explanation.
gaps.proposal: Select a few already relevant phrases per early lesson and provide careful-versus-conversational listening with speaker, variety and register notes. Audit the existing recordings first.
gaps.acceptance: Every phrase is supported or glossed; recordings are checked against a transcript. Variation is labeled, and learners are not told that one reduction is universal.

gaps.title: Routes for different ages and existing abilities
gaps.finding: The usage guide discusses university/research learners, heritage undergraduates and self-study, and permits model-led or analytic study. It is not an age-specific family, child or teen curriculum, and no entry diagnostic was identified.
gaps.effect: Age alone does not reveal whether someone needs speaking, listening, script or grammar support.
gaps.proposal: Use separate entry choices for age, Malayalam understanding/speaking, script literacy, purpose and activity preference. Develop versions of the same objective: caregiver game, teen project, independent adult task, or explicit grammar study.
gaps.acceptance: Routes respond to demonstrated needs and preferences, not fixed learning-style labels. Heritage learners can enter literacy work without repeating skills they already have; beginners still receive prerequisite support.

gaps.title: Additional contemporary communication contexts
gaps.finding: The source period is explicit and several historical facts are already flagged. Existing family, food, travel, office and cultural contexts cover many practical functions. Dedicated activities for current messaging, calls and other learner-selected situations were not identified in the reviewed teaching units.
gaps.effect: Learners with different purposes may want to apply known forms to situations outside the textbook.
